h1: The distillery licence process in India
title: The Distillery Licence Process in India | Craft Beer School
desc: The approvals a new distillery in India typically needs, in the order founders usually meet them, with tips on planning for delays.
teaser: A distillery licence is not one form. It is a sequence of approvals across state and central bodies. The order matters.
standfirst: Getting a distillery licensed in India takes longer than building it. The process differs from state to state and changes often. What follows is the general shape of it, so you know what to ask, not legal advice on what any state currently requires.
sections:
In India, the manufacture and sale of alcoholic drinks for human consumption is regulated mainly by state governments. Each state has its own excise act, rules, licence categories, fees and procedures. A process that takes months in one state can take much longer in another. Some states have periods when they issue few or no new distillery licences.

This is why every founder should work with a licensing consultant or lawyer who knows the current rules in the specific state. Policies, fee structures and licence names change with new excise notifications. Anything you read, including this guide, should be checked against the current notification.

The order varies, but most projects meet these approvals in roughly this sequence:

  1. Policy check and in-principle approval. Confirming the state will consider a new distillery and, in many states, applying for a letter of intent or in-principle approval from the excise department.
  2. Land and building. Land use change if needed, building plan approval and local body permissions.
  3. Environmental consents. Consent to establish from the state pollution control board before construction, then consent to operate before production. Depending on the type and scale of distillery, environmental clearance may also be needed.
  4. Factory, boiler and fire approvals. Factory licence, approval for steam boilers and fire safety clearance.
  5. Manufacturing licence. The excise licence to distil, granted once the plant is built and inspected.
  6. Bonded warehouse. Licensing of the warehouse where spirit matures under bond, with excise control.
  7. Food safety. A licence from the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), which sets standards for alcoholic beverages.
  8. Label and brand registration. Registration of each label and brand with the excise department, often in each state where you plan to sell.

Excise officers treat a distillery as a store of untaxed spirit. The plant design has to support their control. Expect requirements such as locked spirit safes and receivers, meters or dip charts on receivers, secure warehouse access and detailed registers for every movement of spirit.

The records are measured in litres of pure alcohol at a reference temperature. If your new make comes off the still at around 70% ABV, every litre must be measured, temperature corrected and recorded. A plant designed without excise in mind often needs expensive changes before the licence is granted.
Pollution control is often the longest step

Distilleries produce high strength effluent. Pollution control boards typically place them in a high pollution category with strict conditions on treatment and discharge. Many states expect zero liquid discharge from distilleries. The consent to establish usually needs a detailed effluent treatment plan. Our guide to distillery effluent treatment in India explains the options.

Founders who design the effluent plant late, after the stills, often find this approval holds up everything else.

A licence to make spirit does not mean you can sell it everywhere. Each state controls sales within its borders. Selling into another state usually means label registration there, excise permits to move spirit across state lines and working with that state's distribution system. Some states sell through a government corporation, others through private wholesalers. Each has its own price approval and MRP process.

Plan your first markets early. Registering in two or three states is a realistic start for a craft distillery.

We will not quote fees or timelines because both vary so much by state and change often. What we can say is that the sequence above commonly takes longer than founders plan. That time costs money: rent, salaries and interest all run while you wait. Build the licensing period into your budget as a phase of its own.

Many of the approvals ask for the same core documents, so preparing them once saves months. Most applications expect some version of these:

  • Proof of land ownership or lease and land use permission.
  • A detailed project report describing the process, capacity, raw materials and products.
  • A site layout and building plans showing the distillery, warehouse and effluent plant.
  • A process flow diagram with water, steam and effluent streams.
  • Effluent treatment design, usually prepared by a specialist.
  • Details of directors or partners, company registration and financial standing.

A clear process description makes every application easier. Officials need to understand what goes in, what comes out and where the spirit is controlled. If your capacity is stated as, say, 500 litres of pure alcohol a day, every document should use that same figure. Inconsistent numbers across applications cause delays.

Write the eight approvals above down the left side of a page. For your chosen state, note which body grants each one, what documents it needs and what must be in place first. Where you cannot fill a box, that is the first question for a licensing consultant. Knowing how the plant works helps here, because many of these approvals ask you to describe your process, effluent and spirit handling in detail.
faqs: Who issues a distillery licence in India?
The state excise department issues the manufacturing licence, but several other approvals are needed, including pollution control board consents and an FSSAI licence.
How long does a distillery licence take in India?
It varies widely by state and project. Treat licensing as a phase of its own in your plan and budget. Check current timelines with a licensing consultant.
Can a distillery sell its whisky in every state?
No. Each state controls sales within its borders, so you need label registration and permits in each state where you plan to sell.
